options.text: It compresses text into zip files before writing to disk.

options.text: It delays copying memory buffers until a mutation actually occurs.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift not allow integer subscripting on strings like text[0]? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that characters take variable byte lengths in Unicode UTF-8
Explains that finding the nth character requires iterating from the start
Mentions that Swift uses String.Index to avoid misleading developers with hidden O(n) costs

questions.modelAnswer: Swift does not allow integer subscripting on strings because Unicode characters have variable byte lengths in UTF-8. A single visual character can require one byte or many combined bytes. Finding the nth character requires walking from the start of the string, making random access an O(n) operation. Swift requires String.Index to make sure developers understand this traversal cost.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: What is an extended grapheme cluster, and how does canonical equivalence work when comparing strings in Swift? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines an extended grapheme cluster as one or more Unicode scalars producing a single readable character
Explains that canonical equivalence treats characters with the same visual appearance and meaning as equal
Notes that precomposed and decomposed forms compare as equal with ==

questions.modelAnswer: An extended grapheme cluster is a sequence of one or more Unicode scalars that combine to create a single human-readable character. In Swift, string equality comparison uses canonical equivalence. This means that two strings are considered equal if their grapheme clusters have the same visual appearance and linguistic meaning. For example, a precomposed character é matches a decomposed e followed by an accent mark.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between String and Substring in Swift. Why should you convert a Substring to a String before saving it in a long-lived object? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Substring shares the memory buffer of its parent String
Identifies that retaining a Substring prevents the entire parent buffer from being deallocated
States that converting to String(substring) creates an independent buffer

questions.modelAnswer: A Substring is a lightweight slice that reuses the memory buffer of its parent string to make slicing fast. However, holding a reference to a Substring keeps the entire parent string alive in memory. If you slice a small word from a huge document, the entire document remains allocated. Converting the slice to String(substring) creates a new independent buffer, allowing the original document to be freed.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: How does String.endIndex differ from the position of the last character in a string? What happens if you try to subscript text[text.endIndex]? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that endIndex points to the position immediately following the last character
Explains that accessing text[text.endIndex] triggers a fatal runtime crash
Mentions that the final valid character is accessed using index(before: text.endIndex)

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, the endIndex property points to the position immediately after the final character in a string. It represents a past-the-end boundary for half-open ranges. Attempting to access text[text.endIndex] causes a fatal out-of-bounds runtime crash. To access the final character of a non-empty string, you must use text.index(before: text.endIndex).

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: Explain how Swift strings combine value semantics with performance optimization using Copy-on-Write (COW). Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that String is a struct with value semantics
Explains that Copy-on-Write shares the underlying buffer across copies until a mutation occurs
Notes that this optimization eliminates unnecessary memory copying during read-only passes

questions.modelAnswer: Swift strings are value types implemented as structs, keeping independent behavior when passed between functions. Behind the scenes, Swift optimizes memory using Copy-on-Write. Multiple string variables share the same underlying memory buffer until one of them is modified. Only when a mutation occurs does Swift allocate a fresh memory copy, providing excellent performance without sacrificing safety.
